cards.title: Safe Medication Practice
cards.body: Global Nursing Professional Series (GNPS) · Program 3

bullets.label: "The right medication. The right patient. Every time."

cards.title: Welcome to GNPS Program 3
cards.body: Medication administration is one of the most frequent and highest-risk responsibilities in nursing. Every tablet, injection, infusion or topical medicine requires careful assessment, accurate preparation, correct identification and ongoing observation.

bullets.label: This programme develops the essential
bullets.text: This programme develops the essential knowledge, calculation skills, professional attitudes and practical behaviours required to administer medicines safely within your scope of practice.

bullets.label: Explain core concepts and common medication classifications
Understand absorption, distribution, metabolism and elimination
Apply the Medication Rights consistently every time
Calculate common doses accurately and safely
Observe patient response, record and educate effectively

cards.title: WHY THIS MATTERS
cards.body: Nurses Are the Final Safety Check

bullets.label: A medication error can occur at any stage —
bullets.text: A medication error can occur at any stage — prescribing, transcribing, dispensing, preparing, administering or monitoring. Nurses stand as the last line of defence before a medicine reaches the patient.

bullets.label: Safe medication practice depends on knowledge, attention and accountability — every single time.

cards.title: Your Learning Goal
cards.body: Calculate. Prepare. Administer. Monitor. Document.

bullets.label: By the end of Level 1, you should be able to
bullets.text: By the end of Level 1, you should be able to safely manage commonly used medicines while following national standards, organisational procedures and your scope of practice.

bullets.label: FOUNDATION FOR LEVEL 2 — INTERNATIONAL QUALIFIED NURSE

cards.title: Section 1: Foundations of Pharmacology
cards.body: Understanding how medicines work — before you administer them

bullets.label: Generic vs brand names; medication classes
What the body does to the medicine
What the medicine does to the body

cards.title: Pharmacokinetics: ADME
cards.body: Pharmacokinetics describes what the body does to a medicine. Age, hydration, organ function and route of administration can all alter these processes.

bullets.label: Understanding ADME helps nurses anticipate how
bullets.text: Understanding ADME helps nurses anticipate how quickly a medicine will act, how long it will last and what monitoring is required — particularly in patients with liver or kidney impairment.

cards.title: Therapeutic vs Unwanted Effects
cards.body: Every medicine has an intended purpose — but nurses must also monitor for:

bullets.label: Adverse reactions — harmful or unexpected effects
Know the main therapeutic purpose and the important risks of every medicine you administer.

cards.title: Clinical Example
cards.body: Heart Failure & Diuretics

bullets.label: A patient with heart failure is prescribed a diuretic. Before administration, the nurse checks:
The medicine should reduce excess fluid — but may also cause dehydration, low blood pressure or electrolyte imbalance.

cards.title: Section 2: Calculating, Preparing & Administering Medicines
cards.body: Correct calculation + correct technique = safe administration

cards.title: The Rights of Medication Administration
cards.body: These rights create deliberate checks before, during and after administration. Organisations may use different lists — the purpose is always the same.

bullets.label: Additional rights include: reason, assessment, education, evaluation and the patient's right to refuse.

cards.title: Medication Dose Calculations
cards.body: Use an approved method and always check for reasonableness. The core formula:

bullets.label: Required Dose ÷ Available Dose × Available Quantity = Volume to Administer
High-alert medicines requiring a second check

cards.title: Routes of Administration
cards.body: Oral / Sublingual

bullets.label: Most common. Check swallowing ability and crushing restrictions.
Confirm site, angle and needle length. Rotate sites for regular injections.
Fastest onset. Verify concentration, rate, compatibility and line patency.
Technique matters. Confirm correct device use and skin integrity.

cards.title: Section 3: Preventing Errors & Recognising Adverse Reactions
cards.body: Safety continues after the medicine is given

cards.title: Common Causes of Medication Errors
cards.body: Preventing Errors

bullets.label: Most errors are system and process failures — not individual failures. Consistent habits protect patients:
Prepare medicines for one patient at a time
Never administer an unlabelled or damaged product
Perform a second check for high-alert medicines

cards.title: Allergy vs Adverse Drug Reactions
cards.body: Allergy (Immune Response)

bullets.label: Rash, urticaria, angioedema, wheeze, anaphylaxis — can be life-threatening
Bleeding, severe nausea, confusion, hypotension, organ toxicity
Predictable, dose-related — e.g. nausea with opioids, dry mouth with antihistamines

cards.title: Clinical Example
cards.body: Anaphylaxis Response

bullets.label: A patient develops itching, facial swelling and
bullets.text: A patient develops itching, facial swelling and difficulty breathing shortly after IV antibiotic administration. The nurse:

bullets.label: A contraindication is a reason a medicine may
bullets.text: A contraindication is a reason a medicine may be unsuitable — e.g. pregnancy, severe renal impairment, prior serious allergy.

bullets.label: Interactions can occur between medicines, food,
bullets.text: Interactions can occur between medicines, food, alcohol or herbal products. Always review the complete medication history.

bullets.label: Treat new breathing difficulty or facial swelling as a medical emergency — act immediately.

cards.title: Section 4: Accountability, Documentation & Patient Education
cards.body: Safe medication practice is both a clinical and a professional responsibility

cards.title: Professional Accountability
cards.body: A prescriber's order does not remove the nurse's responsibility to question an unsafe or unclear instruction. Nurses are accountable for the entire medication process.

bullets.label: Check the patient and the order

cards.title: Documentation Standards
cards.body: Record what was given, when, by which route and by whom

bullets.label: Document omitted, delayed or refused doses with the reason
Never document before the medicine is actually given
Corrections must follow organisational policy — no erasures
A competent patient may refuse a medicine.
bullets.text: A competent patient may refuse a medicine. Explore concerns, provide information, notify the clinician and document without coercion.

cards.title: Patient Education: Key Components
cards.body: Name & Purpose

bullets.label: Explain what the medicine is and why it has been prescribed
When to take it, how often, and what to do if a dose is missed
Important unwanted effects and what to avoid — food, alcohol, other medicines
Ask the patient to explain instructions in their own words to confirm understanding

cards.title: Clinical Example
cards.body: Mrs Patel & Anticoagulant Education

bullets.label: Mrs Patel is newly prescribed an anticoagulant. The nurse explains:
Why it is needed and how to take it
The importance of not doubling missed doses
Signs of bleeding requiring urgent review
Mrs Patel is asked to explain the instructions back. A misunderstanding is identified and corrected before discharge.
Question any order that appears unsafe or unclear
Respect informed refusal — document without coercion
Use teach-back to confirm patient understanding

cards.title: Programme Summary: What You Have Achieved
cards.body: Pharmacology Foundations

bullets.label: Understand how medicines move through and act on the body
Apply the Rights and calculate doses accurately
Recognise adverse reactions and respond appropriately
Document accurately and educate patients effectively
These capabilities form the foundation for
bullets.text: These capabilities form the foundation for Level 2 — International Qualified Nurse, where medication decisions become more complex within international and multidisciplinary care settings.

cards.title: Safe Medication Practice
cards.body: Global Nursing Professional Series (GNPS) · Program 3

bullets.label: Pharmacology and Medication Safety — Level 1 Qualified Nurse

cards.title: Programme Outline
cards.body: This section establishes the foundational knowledge every nurse needs before safely administering any medicine.

bullets.label: Pharmacology principles, terminology, and medication safety basics
How medicines move through and act on the body
Medication classes, therapeutic effects, and adverse reactions
Applying pharmacological knowledge to real patient scenarios

cards.title: Introduction to Pharmacology
cards.body: Pharmacology is the study of medicines and their effects on the body. Nurses do not need to memorise every medicine — but they must understand the principles behind safe practice.

bullets.label: Understand the clinical reason for every medicine prescribed
Know the mechanism of action and expected physiological response
Anticipate side effects and monitor for adverse reactions
"Safe medication practice begins before the medicine is even prepared."

cards.title: Learning Outcomes
cards.body: After completing this section, you will be able to:

bullets.label: Understand key terms used across clinical and professional settings
Describe how medicines move through the body
Trace the journey from absorption to elimination
Recognise drug classes and their primary therapeutic purposes
Apply knowledge to safe nursing care
Connect pharmacology principles directly to patient assessment and monitoring

cards.title: Medication Names & Classifications
cards.body: Generic vs. Brand Names

bullets.label: Every medicine has a generic name and may have
bullets.text: Every medicine has a generic name and may have one or more brand names. In professional practice, generic names are always preferred — they remain consistent across countries and manufacturers.

cards.title: Pharmacokinetics
cards.body: What the body does to the medicine

bullets.label: Age, hydration, organ function, and route of
bullets.text: Age, hydration, organ function, and route of administration can all alter these processes — making patient assessment before administration essential for every nurse.

cards.title: Pharmacodynamics
cards.body: What the medicine does to the body

bullets.label: Pharmacodynamics explains the mechanism by which a medicine produces its effect. Medicines may:
Activate a receptor or physiological process
Inhibit or prevent a normal body response
Alter the rate or intensity of a physiological function

cards.title: Therapeutic & Unwanted Effects
cards.body: Therapeutic Effect

bullets.label: The intended benefit — the reason the medicine was prescribed
Predictable secondary effects that occur alongside the therapeutic action
Harmful or unexpected responses that require immediate clinical attention
Occurs when a medicine accumulates or is given in excessive amounts — often linked to organ impairment

cards.title: Clinical Example: Diuretics in Heart Failure
cards.body: Scenario

bullets.label: A patient with heart failure is prescribed a diuretic. Before administering, the nurse assesses:
Fluid balance — expected reduction in excess fluid
Recent electrolyte results — risk of hypokalaemia
Pharmacological knowledge guides both safe administration and effective ongoing monitoring.

cards.title: Key Learning Points
cards.body: Anchor your practice in these four principles every time you administer a medicine:

bullets.label: Always understand why each medicine is prescribed before administering it
Prefer generic names in all professional communication for clarity and safety
Consider liver and kidney function — both directly affect how medicines are cleared
Watch for therapeutic outcomes and document any unwanted or adverse effects promptly
"The right medication. The right patient. Every time."

cards.title: Safe Medication Practice
cards.body: Global Nursing Professional Series (GNPS) · Program 3 · Section 2

bullets.label: Calculating, Preparing and Administering Medicines Safely — Level 1 Qualified Nurse

cards.title: Section Overview
cards.body: "The right medication. The right patient. Every time."

bullets.label: Deliberate checks before, during and after administration
Aseptic, focused, one patient at a time

cards.title: Learning Outcomes
cards.body: By the end of this section, you will be able to:

bullets.label: Use the Rights of Medication Administration consistently in every clinical encounter
Perform basic and weight-based medication calculations with confidence and precision
Follow aseptic practice when preparing medicines, checking all product details
Deliver medicines via common routes and monitor the patient after administration

cards.title: The Rights of Medication Administration
cards.body: These deliberate checks form a safety framework applied before, during and after every administration. Organisations may vary the list, but the purpose is consistent.

bullets.label: Verify identity using at least two identifiers
Confirm the drug name matches the order exactly
Confirm appropriateness for this patient and order

cards.title: Extended Rights — Beyond the Basics
cards.body: Modern frameworks extend beyond five rights to strengthen professional accountability.

bullets.label: Record administration promptly and accurately in the patient's record
Know why the medicine is prescribed and assess suitability before giving
Provide clear information to the patient about their medication
Respect the patient's informed decision and document accordingly

cards.title: Medication Calculations
cards.body: The Core Formula

bullets.label: Required Dose ÷ Available Dose × Available Quantity
Always verify your answer is clinically reasonable before proceeding.
Decimal points — misplaced decimals cause 10-fold errors
Unit conversion — convert mg to mcg, or g to mg before calculating
Weight-based doses — paediatric and critical care require extra care
Second check — seek an independent check when policy requires it
When in doubt, calculate twice and ask a colleague before administering.

cards.title: Clinical Example: Applying the Formula
cards.body: Verify ID & Allergy, Administer

bullets.label: This example illustrates how a straightforward
bullets.text: This example illustrates how a straightforward formula, combined with patient identity checks and allergy verification, prevents errors even when the prescribed dose differs from the available concentration.

bullets.label: Verify drug name, dose, route, frequency, and prescriber signature
Confirm label, expiry date, concentration and physical integrity
Prepare in a clean area with minimal interruption — never batch prepare
Unlabelled, damaged or suspicious medicines must never be administered

cards.title: Routes of Administration
cards.body: Route-Specific Responsibilities

bullets.label: Each route carries unique clinical requirements. Before administering, the nurse must:
Confirm personal competence for that route
Assess whether the route is appropriate for this patient
Observe the patient after administration for response or adverse effects
Route errors are a leading cause of serious medication incidents. Always verify before proceeding.

cards.title: Key Takeaways
cards.body: Embed these principles into every medication round — regardless of how busy the clinical environment is.

bullets.label: Use the medication rights every single time — no shortcuts
Verify units, check reasonableness, and seek a second check when required
One patient, clean area, no interruptions, valid labelled products only
Record administration immediately after giving — never before

cards.title: Safe Medication Practice
cards.body: Pharmacology and Medication Safety — Section 3: Preventing Errors and Recognising Adverse Reactions

cards.title: Section Overview
cards.body: Medication safety does not end when a medicine is given. Nurses must continuously observe patients for benefit, side effects, allergy, interactions, and deterioration. Early recognition and prompt action can prevent a mild reaction from becoming a serious emergency.

bullets.label: Why and how to review thoroughly

cards.title: Learning Outcomes
cards.body: What You Will Be Able to Do

bullets.label: Recognise common causes and types of medication errors in clinical practice
Distinguish adverse drug reactions and allergies from expected side effects
Apply knowledge of contraindications and drug interactions when reviewing medicines
Take correct, timely action and complete documentation following a medication incident

cards.title: Medication Errors: Types & Causes
cards.body: Understanding how errors occur is the first step to preventing them.

cards.title: Types of Medication Errors
cards.body: Also Watch For

bullets.label: Incomplete documentation — missing entries create risk for the next clinician
Look-alike packaging — similar labels lead to selection errors
Unclear or verbal orders — always clarify before administration
Every error type maps directly to one of the Rights of Medication Administration — the foundation of safe practice.

cards.title: Contributing Factors to Errors
cards.body: Errors rarely have a single cause. Multiple system and human factors combine to increase risk.

bullets.label: Breaks in concentration during preparation or administration are a leading contributor to errors
Shift work and long hours reduce alertness, increasing the likelihood of missed steps
Failing to verify patient identity before administration is a preventable and serious risk
Ambiguous or illegible prescriptions must always be queried before a medicine is given

cards.title: Allergy vs. Adverse Drug Reactions
cards.body: Allergic Reaction

bullets.label: Involves an immune response. Can range from mild to life-threatening.
Unwanted effects that are not immune-mediated but still require prompt assessment.
Low blood pressure or organ toxicity
Always distinguish a known, expected side
bullets.text: Always distinguish a known, expected side effect from a new, potentially serious reaction. When in doubt — assess, escalate, and document.

cards.title: Contraindications & Drug Interactions
cards.body: A contraindication is any reason a medicine may be unsuitable or unsafe for a particular patient.

cards.title: What to Review Before Administering
cards.body: Common Contraindications

bullets.label: Severe renal or hepatic impairment — affects drug clearance
Always review the complete medication history —
bullets.text: Always review the complete medication history — including over-the-counter medicines, herbal supplements, and alcohol use — before administering any drug.

cards.title: Responding to a Medication Incident
cards.body: If an error or serious adverse reaction occurs, patient safety always comes first.

bullets.label: Concealing an error places the patient at
bullets.text: Concealing an error places the patient at continued risk and is a serious professional and legal breach. Transparent reporting enables system improvements that protect future patients.

cards.title: Clinical Example: Anaphylaxis Response
cards.body: Recognising and acting on an acute allergic reaction — step by step

cards.title: Case in Practice
cards.body: Shortly after receiving an intravenous antibiotic, a patient develops itching, facial swelling, and difficulty breathing.

bullets.label: Immediately cease administration of the suspected causative agent
Activate emergency response; notify the medical team immediately
Position the patient, administer oxygen, follow emergency medication protocol
Record the event fully and update the allergy record to prevent re-exposure

cards.title: Key Learning Points
cards.body: 🔍 Assess Before & After

bullets.label: Always assess the patient before administering and monitor closely afterwards for any change
New breathing difficulty, swelling, or sudden deterioration must be treated as an emergency — act immediately
Check all medicines, foods, and supplements for possible interactions before administration
Report all errors and near misses — transparent reporting protects the next patient
These principles align directly with NCLEX Safe
bullets.text: These principles align directly with NCLEX Safe and Effective Care Environment competencies — practise applying them to clinical scenarios.

decks.title: Accountability, Documentation and Patient Education
decks.sourceFile: GNPS Program 3 - Level 1 - Section 4 Qualified Nurse - Presentation deck.pptx

cards.title: Section 4: Accountability, Documentation & Patient Education
cards.body: GNPS Program 3 – Safe Medication Practice | Level 1: Qualified Nurse

cards.title: Learning Outcomes
cards.body: By the end of this section, you will be able to:

bullets.label: Explain your professional responsibilities in medication administration
Record medication care accurately, promptly and in the correct sequence
Respect the patient's right to information and to refuse treatment
Deliver clear, effective medication education using best-practice methods

cards.title: Professional Accountability
cards.body: A prescriber's order does not remove the nurse's responsibility. You are accountable at every stage of the medication process.

bullets.label: Check the order for accuracy and safety
Prepare and give the medicine safely
Observe the patient's response and escalate concerns
Key principle: Always question any order that appears unsafe, unclear or outside your scope of practice.

cards.title: Accurate Medication Documentation
cards.body: What must be recorded?

bullets.label: What was administered – medicine name and dose
When it was given – date and time
How it was given – route of administration
Always record the reason for any missed or delayed dose, along with any relevant follow-up actions taken.
Never document before the medicine has been given.

cards.title: Consent, Information & the Right to Refuse
cards.body: Every competent patient has the legal and ethical right to make informed decisions about their treatment — including the right to decline it.

bullets.label: Explain the medicine's purpose, expected benefit and key risks in plain language
Listen to the patient's concerns and address misconceptions without pressure
Inform the appropriate clinician when a patient refuses a prescribed medicine
Record the refusal, the reason given, information provided and follow-up actions

cards.title: Delivering Effective Patient Education
cards.body: Medicine Name & Purpose

bullets.label: What it is called and why it has been prescribed
How much, how often and how to take or apply it
Important effects to watch for and what to avoid
How to store the medicine and which symptoms require urgent review
Use plain language, provide written information
bullets.text: Use plain language, provide written information where possible, and always confirm understanding using the teach-back method.

cards.title: The Teach-Back Method
cards.body: Teach-back is the gold standard for confirming patient understanding. It shifts the focus from what you said to what the patient understood.

bullets.label: Teach-back reduces medication errors, improves
bullets.text: Teach-back reduces medication errors, improves adherence and supports safe discharge — especially for new or complex medicines.

cards.title: Clinical Example: Mrs Patel
cards.body: A newly prescribed anticoagulant — how should the nurse approach education?

bullets.label: Describe why the anticoagulant has been prescribed and how it works
Clarify when to take it and what to do if a dose is missed — never double a dose
Explain signs of bleeding that require urgent medical review
Ask Mrs Patel to repeat the instructions — correct misunderstandings before discharge

cards.title: Key Learning Points
cards.body: Remember These Principles

bullets.label: Question any order that appears unsafe, unclear or ambiguous
Document only after the medicine has been administered
Respect informed refusal — explore, notify and document
Use teach-back to verify patient understanding every time

cards.title: Programme Summary & What's Next
cards.body: By completing GNPS Program 3 – Level 1, you have built essential foundations in safe medication practice.

bullets.label: Understanding how medicines work in the body
Accurate dose calculation and the rights of administration
Identifying and responding to unwanted drug effects
Communicating medicine information clearly and effectively
Coming next: Level 2 – International Qualified
bullets.text: Coming next: Level 2 – International Qualified Nurse, where medication decisions become more complex and are applied within international systems and multidisciplinary care.
